meta.title: Bengali A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Bengali → English (see the Bengali, recall the meaning) and English → Bengali (see an English meaning, recall the Bengali). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to manage simple, routine exchanges of information on familiar matters — personal and family information, shopping, the local area, work — and to describe in simple terms their background, their surroundings and what they immediately need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for learners of Bengali, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 252 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — relatives and the people around you, work and study, clothes and shopping, more food and cooking, the furniture of a home, the town, the countryside, the seasons and the points of the compass, travel, health and the body, feelings and character, free time, telling what happened and when, giving an opinion, the months and the numbers to a crore, and the everyday verbs of moving, dressing and doing — and the other 498 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Bengali, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. The deck teaches the standard colloquial language (cholito bhasha) shared by West Bengal and Bangladesh; where an everyday word differs between the two — জল and পানি for water, নমস্কার and সালাম for a greeting — both are taught. Every headword is printed in the Bengali script with a romanisation beneath it, Wiktionary's own (ô for the open o of the inherent vowel, ō where the o-sign is written, a dot under the retroflex letters, ẏ and ẇ for the glides: kôra, bhalō), so the deck can be studied before the script is fluent; the Bengali Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the script itself. Bengali has no grammatical gender. The 495 nouns show their definite form ('the …', with -টা), their plural and their genitive ('of …'); the 69 verbs show their present, their past and their 'having done' form, where the stem's vowel changes and the irregular verbs show, and behind the All forms fold every tense by person, at the three levels of address — তুই intimate, তুমি familiar, আপনি polite. Real example sentences come with 523 of the 750 words, three apiece for 283 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, forms and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.

২০০০-এর দশকের মাঝামাঝি সময়ে বিদ্যুৎচালিত রিকশা বাংলাদেশে আসা শুরু করার পর থেকেই দেশে এগুলো চালাতে দেওয়া উচিত কি না তা নিয়ে অনেক বিতর্ক হয়ে আসছে।
Whether electricity-charged rickshaws should be allowed to operate in the country has been a much-debated issue since they started coming to Bangladesh in the mid-2000s.
নীতিনির্ধারকবৃন্দ এবং যারা নিজেদের যানবাহনে চলাফেরা করেন তারা নিম্ন আয়ের মানুষের জীবন সহজ করার জন্য রিকশার অবদান নাও বুঝতে পারেন তবে যারা রিকশা ব্যবহার করেন তারা এটি ঠিকই অনুভব করেন।
Policymakers and the people who ride their own vehicles might not understand the contribution of rickshaws to easing the lives of low-income people, but those who use them feel it.
